questions.question: What is the Publish/Subscribe (Pub/Sub) pattern?

options.text: Direct point-to-point communication between two services
Publishers send messages to topics; subscribers receive messages from topics they're interested in
Synchronous request-response communication pattern
Database replication pattern for consistency

questions.explanation: Pub/Sub decouples publishers from subscribers through topics/channels. Publishers don't know who receives messages; subscribers don't know who sends them. Google Cloud Pub/Sub handles millions of messages per second for YouTube notifications. This enables loose coupling, independent scaling, and easy addition of new consumers without modifying producers.

questions.question: Which benefits does Pub/Sub provide? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Loose coupling between services
Guaranteed message ordering across all subscribers
Easy addition of new subscribers without changing publishers
Scalability through parallel message processing

questions.explanation: Pub/Sub provides loose coupling (publishers and subscribers are independent), easy extensibility (add subscribers anytime without code changes), and scalability (multiple subscribers process in parallel). Message ordering is NOT guaranteed by default—messages may arrive out of order across subscribers or even within a subscriber without proper partitioning. Kafka provides ordering within partitions only.

questions.question: How does Pub/Sub differ from a message queue?

options.text: Pub/Sub delivers messages to all subscribers; queues deliver to one consumer
Pub/Sub is synchronous; queues are asynchronous
Pub/Sub cannot persist messages; queues always persist
There is no functional difference between them

questions.explanation: Key difference: Pub/Sub broadcasts to ALL subscribers (fan-out)—if 5 services subscribe, all 5 get the message. Message queues deliver each message to ONE consumer (competing consumers pattern)—if 5 workers listen, only 1 processes each message. Both are asynchronous and can persist messages. Use Pub/Sub for notifications; use queues for work distribution.

questions.question: A microservices system uses Pub/Sub for order events. The 'order.created' event needs to trigger inventory update, email notification, and analytics. How many subscribers should exist?

options.text: 1 subscriber handling all three tasks sequentially
3 subscribers, one for each concern
0 subscribers—use direct synchronous API calls instead
Depends only on message volume, not on concerns

questions.explanation: Each concern (inventory, email, analytics) should be a separate subscriber. This follows single responsibility principle, allows independent scaling (analytics might need more capacity than email), and prevents one slow handler from blocking others. If email service is slow, inventory updates still happen immediately. Shopify uses this pattern for order processing.

questions.question: What is a 'topic' in Pub/Sub systems?

options.text: A database table for storing messages
A named channel where publishers send messages and subscribers listen
A message queue with FIFO ordering
A group of subscribers with shared state

questions.explanation: A topic is a named channel/category for messages. Publishers send to topics ('orders', 'payments', 'user-events'); subscribers subscribe to topics of interest. Topics enable message routing without direct publisher-subscriber coupling. AWS SNS topics, Kafka topics, and Google Pub/Sub topics all follow this model. Topic design is crucial—too few creates noise, too many creates management overhead.

questions.question: What happens to a Pub/Sub message if no subscribers exist for a topic?

options.text: Message is always queued until a subscriber appears
Behavior depends on implementation—may be discarded or stored
Publisher always receives an error
Message is automatically returned to publisher

questions.explanation: Behavior varies by implementation: Redis Pub/Sub discards messages with no subscribers (fire-and-forget). Kafka retains messages regardless of subscribers (log-based). Google Pub/Sub requires at least one subscription to retain messages. AWS SNS discards if no subscriptions exist. Understand your system's semantics—this affects whether you can add subscribers retroactively.

questions.question: Which challenges exist with Pub/Sub? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Message ordering across subscribers
Debugging message flow across services
Handling subscriber failures and retries
Tight coupling between publishers and subscribers

questions.explanation: Pub/Sub challenges include: ordering (messages may arrive out of order without careful partitioning), debugging (tracing messages across services requires distributed tracing—harder than following synchronous call stacks), and failure handling (what if subscriber crashes mid-processing?). Pub/Sub REDUCES coupling, not increases it—that's its primary benefit. The complexity is the price of loose coupling.

questions.question: A subscriber processes messages slowly, causing backlog. What pattern helps?

options.text: Delete the slow subscriber from the system
Consumer groups with multiple instances sharing the load
Increase publisher message rate
Reduce the number of topics

questions.explanation: Consumer groups allow multiple instances of a subscriber to share message processing. Each message goes to one instance in the group, enabling horizontal scaling of slow consumers. Kafka consumer groups, SQS with multiple readers, and RabbitMQ competing consumers all implement this pattern. Scale consumers independently based on their processing capacity and backlog.

questions.question: True or False: In Pub/Sub, publishers must know about all subscribers.

options.text: True - publishers need subscriber addresses for delivery
False - publishers only know about topics, not subscribers

questions.explanation: Publishers are completely decoupled from subscribers—they only know about topics. New subscribers can be added without any publisher changes. This is a core benefit of Pub/Sub: the analytics team can subscribe to order events without the order service knowing or caring. This enables independent team velocity and system evolution.

questions.question: What is 'fan-out' in Pub/Sub?

options.text: Reducing message size through compression
One message being delivered to multiple subscribers
Combining multiple messages into one
Load balancing across multiple publishers

questions.explanation: Fan-out means one published message is delivered to all subscribers of that topic. If 5 services subscribe to 'order.created', each receives a copy of every order event. AWS SNS to SQS fan-out is a common pattern: one SNS topic fans out to multiple SQS queues for different processing pipelines. This enables event-driven architectures where multiple systems react to the same business events.

questions.question: A Pub/Sub system needs to ensure each subscriber processes messages in the order they were published. Which approach helps?

options.text: Use multiple topics for different message types
Partition by key and ensure single consumer per partition
Increase subscriber count for faster processing
Ordering is fundamentally impossible in Pub/Sub systems

questions.explanation: Partitioning by key (e.g., order_id, user_id) ensures related messages go to the same partition. With one consumer per partition, ordering is maintained for that key. Kafka uses this approach: messages with the same key go to the same partition, and partitions are consumed in order. This gives you ordering where it matters (per-entity) while allowing parallelism across entities.

questions.question: Which systems implement the Pub/Sub pattern? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Apache Kafka
Google Cloud Pub/Sub
Redis Pub/Sub
Amazon SNS

questions.explanation: All listed implement Pub/Sub with different characteristics: Kafka (distributed log with retention, ordering within partitions), Google Pub/Sub (managed, global, at-least-once), Redis Pub/Sub (in-memory, no persistence, fire-and-forget), SNS (AWS managed, integrates with SQS/Lambda). Choose based on durability needs, ordering requirements, and operational preferences.
